title: Accuracy, precision, significant figures and error
blurb: Tell accuracy from precision, match each error type to its fix, calculate percent error and count significant figures.
question: A student weighs a certified 50.0 g standard mass three times and gets 48.2 g, 48.3 g and 48.2 g. Are her results accurate, precise, both or neither, what kind of error is most likely, and what is her percent error?

teach.body: Formally, accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true or accepted value, and precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other (and how fine the instrument's scale is). In plain English: accuracy asks 'did you hit the target?' and precision asks 'did you hit the same spot every time?' A set of results can be precise without being accurate, which is exactly what the exam likes to test.

teach.caption: Scattered results can still average close to the true value: accurate on average, but not precise.
Averaging more trials does NOT remove a systematic error: every reading is shifted the same way.

teach.body: Percent error measures how far a result is from the accepted value: percent error = |measured - accepted| ÷ accepted x 100%. Always divide by the ACCEPTED value, never by your own measurement. The vertical bars mean 'take the size of the difference', so percent error is reported as a positive number whether you measured too high or too low.

items: Accepted value: 50.0 g. Average measured value: (48.2 + 48.3 + 48.2) ÷ 3 = 48.2 g (to one decimal place).
Multiply by 100%: percent error = 3.6%. The readings agree closely (precise) but sit low (not accurate), pointing to a systematic error such as an unzeroed balance.

head: Rule
Example
Sig figs
rows: Trailing zeros with a decimal point count
Trailing zeros, no decimal point: do not count
teach.caption: 250 is ambiguous, so by the rule above it is treated as 2 significant figures. Writing 250. or 2.50 x 10² shows 3.

teach.body: When you read a scale, record every certain digit plus ONE estimated digit beyond the smallest marking: a cylinder marked every 1 mL is read to 0.1 mL (for example 36.3 mL). In calculations, multiplying or dividing gives an answer with the FEWEST significant figures of the inputs; adding or subtracting gives the FEWEST decimal places.

steps.label: Calibrate
steps.sub: Zero (tare) the balance; check against a standard

steps.label: Use correct technique
steps.sub: Eye level, bottom of meniscus: no parallax

teach.caption: The first two steps attack systematic error; the last two attack random error.

teach.body: Marcus, a CNA applying to nursing school, tests a lab thermometer in an ice bath whose accepted temperature is 0.0 °C. Five readings: 1.9, 2.0, 2.1, 2.0 and 2.0 °C. All are within 0.1 °C of 2.0 °C, so they are precise. All are about 2 °C too high, so they are not accurate. The error is systematic (the same direction every time), so taking more readings will not fix it: recalibrating the thermometer will.

teach.text: Don't swap the terms: ACCURACY = close to the true value; PRECISION = close to each other. Leading zeros (0.00xx) are never significant. And percent error divides by the ACCEPTED value: dividing by your measured value gives a near-miss answer that looks right.

items: Accuracy: close to the accepted value. Precision: repeated results close together.
Systematic error shifts every result the same way and hurts accuracy; fix it by calibrating.
Random error scatters results and hurts precision; reduce it by repeating trials and averaging.
Leading zeros never count; trailing zeros count only with a decimal point.
x and ÷: fewest significant figures. + and -: fewest decimal places.

summary: You can now classify a set of results as accurate, precise, both or neither, tell systematic from random error and choose the right fix for each. You can also calculate percent error and apply the significant-figure rules to readings and calculations.

A.q: A certified mass has an accepted value of 50.0 g. Which set of three readings is precise but NOT accurate?
A.why: 45.1, 45.0 and 45.2 g agree within 0.2 g (precise) but are all about 5 g below 50.0 g (not accurate).

whyNot.0: These readings are close together AND close to 50.0 g: both precise and accurate.
whyNot.1: These average about 50.0 g but are widely spread: accurate on average, not precise.
whyNot.3: These are widely spread and average well below 50.0 g: neither precise nor accurate.

A.q: A 20.0 g standard mass reads 19.4 g on a lab balance. What is the percent error?

whyNot.0: 3.1% comes from dividing by the measured value (0.6 ÷ 19.4). Divide by the accepted value.
whyNot.2: 0.6 is the difference in grams, not a percentage of the accepted value.
whyNot.3: 97% is the measured value as a percentage of the accepted value, not the error.

A.q: How many significant figures are in the measurement 0.04050 g?
A.why: Leading zeros (0.0) never count. The 4, the zero between 4 and 5, the 5 and the trailing zero after the decimal point all count: 4 significant figures.

whyNot.0: This drops the trailing zero, but a trailing zero after a decimal point is significant.
whyNot.2: This counts one of the leading zeros. Leading zeros are placeholders, never significant.
whyNot.3: This counts every digit, including the leading zeros.

B.q: A balance was never zeroed and reads 0.5 g high on every measurement. Which describes this error?
B.why: An error in the same direction every time is systematic, and it moves results away from the true value, so it lowers accuracy.

whyNot.1: Random error varies unpredictably; this error is the same 0.5 g every time.
whyNot.2: A constant offset leaves the readings just as close to each other, so precision is not the main casualty.
whyNot.3: The effect on accuracy is right, but a consistent one-direction error is systematic, not random.

B.q: A graduated cylinder is marked every 1 mL. The bottom of the meniscus sits about three-tenths of the way from the 36 mL line to the 37 mL line. What should be recorded?
B.why: Record all certain digits plus one estimated digit beyond the smallest marking: with 1 mL markings, read to 0.1 mL, so 36.3 mL.

whyNot.0: This drops the estimated digit, throwing away information the scale can give.
whyNot.1: This rounds up to the next line instead of estimating between the lines.
whyNot.2: This claims a second estimated digit (0.01 mL) that a 1 mL scale cannot support.

B.q: Reaction times in a study vary unpredictably from trial to trial. Which change best reduces this random error?
options: Recalibrate the timer against a standard
Record each time to more decimal places
Repeat the trials and average results
Read the display from the same angle
B.why: Random error is unpredictable scatter. Repeating trials and averaging smooths it out.

whyNot.0: Calibration corrects a systematic offset, not unpredictable scatter.
whyNot.1: Extra decimal places do not make scattered results agree; they can claim false precision.
whyNot.3: A consistent viewing angle prevents parallax, a systematic error, not random scatter.

C.q: A sample has a mass of 12.45 g and a volume of 3.1 mL. How should its density be reported?
C.why: 12.45 ÷ 3.1 = 4.016... For division, keep the fewest significant figures of the inputs: 3.1 has 2, so report 4.0 g/mL.

whyNot.1: This keeps 4 significant figures, set by 12.45, but the less certain value (3.1) limits the answer.
whyNot.3: This keeps 3 significant figures; division keeps the fewest of the inputs, which is 2.

C.q: A student adds 25.1 mL, 3.256 mL and 0.12 mL of solution to a flask. How should the total volume be reported?
C.why: 25.1 + 3.256 + 0.12 = 28.476. For addition, keep the fewest decimal places of the inputs: 25.1 has one, so 28.5 mL.

whyNot.1: This rounds to zero decimal places, but 25.1 allows one.
whyNot.2: This keeps two decimal places (from 0.12), but the least precise value, 25.1, has one.
whyNot.3: This reports the raw calculator total, claiming more precision than the 25.1 mL reading has.

C.q: Which statement about measurement is INCORRECT?
options: Zeros between digits in 4.007 are significant
The trailing zero in 3.50 is significant
Averaging repeated trials reduces random error
C.why: Leading zeros are placeholders and are never significant: 0.0072 has 2 significant figures. So this statement is the incorrect one.

whyNot.1: This is correct: zeros sandwiched between nonzero digits count, so 4.007 has 4.
whyNot.2: This is correct: a trailing zero after a decimal point counts, so 3.50 has 3.
whyNot.3: This is correct: averaging smooths out unpredictable scatter.

reteach.title: Accuracy and precision at the free-throw line
reteach.question: Picture three basketball players each taking ten free throws. How do their shots show the difference between accuracy and precision?

blocks.body: Jamal's shots all hit the same spot on the left side of the rim and bounce out: very consistent (precise) but missing (not accurate), like a balance that always reads 2 g low. Destiny's shots swish through every time: precise AND accurate. Kevin's shots land all over the rim, some in, some out: his average position is near the hoop, but he is not precise. To fix Jamal, adjust his aim (calibrate). To fix Kevin, practice more and average out the wobble (repeat trials).

blocks.text: Consistency is not correctness. Results that agree with each other can all be wrong by the same amount: that is precision without accuracy.

explain.body: Accuracy is closeness to the accepted value. Precision is closeness of repeated measurements to each other. You need an accepted value to judge accuracy, but only repeated readings to judge precision.

options: a measurement is to the accepted value
repeated readings are to each other
a result is to the predicted value
an average is to the median value
test.why: Precision is the agreement of repeated measurements with one another.

whyNot.0: Closeness to the accepted value is accuracy.
whyNot.2: Comparing a result with a prediction tests a hypothesis; it is not precision.
whyNot.3: Mean vs median describes the shape of a data set, not measurement precision.

explain.body: Systematic error pushes every reading the same way (uncalibrated balance, reading from above) and hurts accuracy. Random error scatters readings unpredictably and hurts precision. Calibrate for the first; repeat and average for the second.

test.q: A balance reads about 1.2 g high on every weighing. Which action corrects this error?
test.why: A constant one-direction offset is a systematic error, which is corrected by calibrating the instrument.

whyNot.0: Every repeat is shifted by the same 1.2 g, so repeating does not remove it.
whyNot.2: The average of readings that are all 1.2 g high is still 1.2 g high.
whyNot.3: More decimal places do not change an offset that affects every reading.

explain.body: Percent error = |measured - accepted| ÷ accepted x 100%. Subtract, take the size of the difference, divide by the ACCEPTED value, then multiply by 100.

test.q: A student measures 9.5 mL of a liquid whose accepted volume is 10.0 mL. What is her percent error?

whyNot.0: 5.3% divides by the measured value (0.5 ÷ 9.5) instead of the accepted value.
whyNot.1: 0.5 is the difference in mL, not a percentage.
whyNot.2: 95% is the measured value as a percentage of the accepted value.

explain.body: Nonzero digits count. Zeros between nonzero digits count. Leading zeros never count. Trailing zeros count only when there is a decimal point.

test.q: Which measurement has exactly three significant figures?
test.why: In 0.0450 the leading zeros do not count; the 4, 5 and the trailing zero after the decimal point do: 3 significant figures.

whyNot.0: Leading zeros never count, leaving 4 and 5: 2 significant figures.
whyNot.1: 4, the sandwiched 0, 5 and the trailing 0 all count: 4 significant figures.
whyNot.3: Without a decimal point the trailing zeros do not count: 2 significant figures.
